claim: Mid-infrared stimulation (MIRS) causes non-thermal modulation of brain functions.
source: Recent reports suggest that mid-infrared stimulation (MIRS) causes non-thermal modulation of brain functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to recent reports in the literature.

claim: MIRS applied to the pretectal nucleus lentiformis mesencephali (nLM) altered eye movements by modulating a specific gain depending on the strength of visual inputs.
source: We found MIRS altered eye movements by modulating a specific gain depending on the strength of visual inputs, in a manner different than the effect of ES.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the study comparing MIRS and ES effects on eye movements.

claim: MIRS could either excite or inhibit neuronal activity in the same pretectal neuron depending on its ongoing sensory responsiveness levels.
source: Simultaneous extracellular recordings and stimulation showed that MIRS could either excite and inhibit the neuronal activity in the same pretectal neuron depending on its ongoing sensory responsiveness levels in awake-behaving animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by simultaneous recording and stimulation experiments in awake-behaving animals.

claim: MIRS modulates the resonance of a carbonyl group of the potassium channel, critical to action potential generation.
source: Computational simulations suggest that MIRS modulates the resonance of a carbonyl group of the potassium channel, critical to the action potential generation, altering neuronal responses to sensory inputs and as a consequence, guiding behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on computational simulations using molecular dynamics methods.

claim: Deep brain and transcranial electromagnetic stimulation directly alter neuronal excitability and connectivity, and their use in clinical settings is widespread.
source: For example, deep brain and transcranial electromagnetic stimulation directly alter neuronal excitability and connectivity, and their use in clinical settings is widespread (Krauss et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krauss et al., 2021.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation has recently extended the toolkit to excite or inhibit specific groups of neurons selectively, but relies on genetic manipulations that currently limit its clinical application.
source: Optogenetic stimulation has recently extended the toolkit to excite or inhibit specific groups of neurons selectively, but relies on genetic manipulations that currently limit its clinical application (Deisseroth, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deisseroth, 2015.

claim: Near-infrared wavelength stimulation (NIRS) can excite neuronal responses in vitro.
source: Initial studies have shown that near-infrared wavelength stimulation (NIRS) can excite neuronal responses in vitro (Izzo et al., 2008; Albert et al., 2012; Shapiro et al., 2012; Entwisle et al., 2016) and in vivo (Wells et al., 2005; Wells et al., 2007a; Wells et al., 2007b; Richter et al., 2008; Xia et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Near-infrared wavelength stimulation (NIRS) can excite neuronal responses in vivo.
source: Initial studies have shown that near-infrared wavelength stimulation (NIRS) can excite neuronal responses in vitro (Izzo et al., 2008; Albert et al., 2012; Shapiro et al., 2012; Entwisle et al., 2016) and in vivo (Wells et al., 2005; Wells et al., 2007a; Wells et al., 2007b; Richter et al., 2008; Xia et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: NIRS can inhibit neuronal firing.
source: Interestingly, there are also reports that NIRS can inhibit neuronal firing (Cayce et al., 2011; Duke et al., 2012; Duke et al., 2013; Horváth et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MIRS can exert non-thermal effects on ion channels, and lead to gain modulation of action potentials based on current injections in the vitro slice preparation.
source: MIRS can exert non-thermal effects on ion channels, and lead to gain modulation of action potentials based on current injections in the vitro slice preparation (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: MIRS can enhance spontaneous neuronal activities in anesthetized animals.
source: MIRS can enhance spontaneous neuronal activities (Zhang et al., 2021) and sensory responses (Tan et al., 2022) in anesthetized animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: MIRS can enhance sensory responses in anesthetized animals.
source: MIRS can enhance spontaneous neuronal activities (Zhang et al., 2021) and sensory responses (Tan et al., 2022) in anesthetized animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2022.

claim: MIRS accelerates associative learning in mice.
source: Consequently, prior reports show how MIRS accelerates associative learning in mice (Zhang et al., 2021), and regulates startle responses in larval zebrafish (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: MIRS regulates startle responses in larval zebrafish.
source: Consequently, prior reports show how MIRS accelerates associative learning in mice (Zhang et al., 2021), and regulates startle responses in larval zebrafish (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: The pretectal nucleus lentiformis mesencephali (nLM) is homologous to the nucleus of the optic tract and highly conserved across all vertebrates.
source: The nLM is homologous to the nucleus of the optic tract and highly conserved across all vertebrates (Fite, 1985; McKenna and Wallman, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fite, 1985 and McKenna and Wallman, 1985.

claim: The majority of nLM neurons prefer slow velocity and become excited by visual motion in the temporal-to-nasal direction.
source: The majority of nLM neurons prefer slow velocity and become excited by visual motion in the temporal-to-nasal direction, while other neurons are predominantly sensitive to the nasal-to-temporal, or vertical motion (Winterson and Brauth, 1985; Wylie and Frost, 1996; Fu et al., 1998; Wylie and Crowder, 2000; Cao et al., 2004; Wylie et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Reversible inactivation or electrolytic lesions of the nLM impair generating horizontal OKN.
source: Reversible inactivation or electrolytic lesions of the nLM impair generating horizontal OKN (Fite et al., 1979; Gioanni et al., 1983; Yang et al., 2008a; Yang et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MIRS significantly speeded up pursuit velocities in slow phases evoked by 8 deg/s grating motion along both T-N and N-T directions.
source: MIRS significantly speeded up pursuit velocities in slow phases evoked by 8 deg/s grating motion along both T-N and N-T directions, in the individual and group animals.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: During 8 deg/s grating motion in the T-N direction, MIRS significantly increased pursuit velocity from 4.78±0.22 deg/s to 6.44±0.38 deg/s (n=20 pigeons, p=8.86×10–5).
source: Once MIRS was turned on, animals significantly fasted their pursuit performance (velocity: 6.44±0.38 deg/s; n=20 pigeons, p=8.86×10–5, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: During 8 deg/s grating motion in the N-T direction, MIRS significantly increased pursuit velocity from –0.99±0.06 deg/s to –1.48±0.08 deg/s (n=20 pigeons, p=2.54×10–4).
source: When MIRS was turned on, animals again significantly fasted their eye movements to pursue in the N-T direction (velocity: –1.48±0.08 deg/s; n=20 pigeons, p=2.54×10–4, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Asymmetry between the N-T and T-N OKN has been widely observed in lateral-eyed vertebrates.
source: There was asymmetry between the N-T and T-N OKN, which has been widely observed in lateral-eyed vertebrates (rabbits: Collewijn, 1969; pigeons: Zolotilina et al., 1995; rats: Harvey et al., 1997; mice: Kodama and du Lac, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research in different species.

claim: Electrical stimulation (ES) in the nLM caused a unidirectional deflection of pursuit eye movements toward the T-N direction, independent of direction of grating motion.
source: Unlike MIRS, ES can evoke pursuit eye movements towards the T-N direction, independent of the direction of grating motion
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing ES to MIRS.

claim: Gain modulation intensity of MIRS on pursuit eye movements during the slow phase depended on the strength of visual inputs (F(4,79)=6.66, p=0.0001).
source: One-way ANOVA analyses revealed that gain modulation intensity of MIRS on pursuit eye movements during the slow phase depended on the strength of visual inputs (F(4,79)=6.66, p=0.0001), in a manner different than the unidirectional modulation of ES (F(4,25)=0.25, p=0.9094).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: 37 out of 43 recorded nLM neurons showed significant visual response changes during 10 mW MIRS (p<0.01).
source: There are 37/43 neurons showed significant visual response changes in pursuit when MIRS at 10 mW applied (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: All recorded nLM cells have been modulated by corollary discharge signals during saccadic eye movements: their firing rates were inhibited during saccades.
source: All recorded nLM cells have been modulated by corollary discharge signals during saccadic eye movements: their firing rates were inhibited during saccades, confirming prior report (Yang et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and confirmed by a citation to prior research.

claim: During MIRS, nearly all neurons showed a further potentiation of their preferred direction visual responses (mean ± SD: 59.02±29.59 spikes/s, n=33 neurons, p=1.76×10–6).
source: During MIRS, nearly all neurons showed a further potentiation of their preferred direction visual responses (Figure 3C, mean ± SD: 59.02±29.59 spikes/s, n=33 neurons, p=1.76×10–6, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: During MIRS, neurons showed a further inhibition in their null direction visual responses (29.16±21.23 spikes/s, n=24 neurons, p=3.96×10–4).
source: and a further inhibition in their null direction visual responses (Figure 3D, 29.16±21.23 spikes/s, n=24 neurons, p=3.96×10–4; two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase of visual responses to the grating motion at 8 deg/s in the preferred direction was significantly larger than 2 deg/s in that direction (8 deg/s: 15.63% ± 1.72%, n=33 neurons; 2 deg/s: 5.25% ± 2.92%, n=13 neurons; p=0.02).
source: During MIRS, the increase of visual responses to the grating motion at 8 deg/s in the preferred direction was significantly larger than 2 deg/s in that direction (Figure 4B, mean ± SEM, 8 deg/s: 15.63% ± 1.72% (n1=33 neurons); 2 deg/s: 5.25% ± 2.92% (n2=13 neurons); n1 vs. n2 p=0.02, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Neuronal activities to still grating failed to show any significant changes during MIRS (mean ± SEM, –4.15% ± 3.87%, n=6 neurons, p=0.37).
source: During MIRS, these neuronal activities to still grating failed to show any significant changes (Figure 4B, mean ± SEM, –4.15% ± 3.87%, n=6 neurons, p=0.37, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test,).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The MIRS output power can effectively modify effects on eye movements in both the T-N and N-T directions at the p<0.05 for the four output powers (F(3, 140)=3.4, p=0.0196).
source: A one-way ANOVA analysis further confirmed that the MIRS output power can effectively modify effects on eye movements in both the T-N and N-T directions at the p<0.05 for the four output powers (F(3, 140)=3.4, p=0.0196).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: MIRS power had a significant effect on evoked responses of the recorded nLM cells to grating motion stimuli (One-way ANOVA, F(3,80)=7.92, p=0.0001).
source: Like behavioral responses, MIRS power had a significant effect on evoked responses of the recorded nLM cells to grating motion stimuli (One-way ANOVA, F(3,80)=7.92, p=0.0001).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The evoked pursuit velocity did not vary substantially as a function of MIRS duration (n30s=5 MIRS times, n120s=20 MIRS times, p=0.8651).
source: The evoked pursuit velocity did not vary substantially as a function of MIRS duration (Figure 4H, n30s=5 MIRS times, n120s=20 MIRS times, p=0.8651, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: There were no significant changes in pursuit velocities during MIRS once the fiber applied in the OKN-irrelevant nuclei (TeO: n=6 MIRS times in 3 pigeons, p=0.31; nRt: n=5 MIRS times in 3 pigeons, p=0.63).
source: There were no significant changes in pursuit velocities during MIRS once the fiber applied in the OKN-irrelevant nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D, TeO: n=6 MIRS times in 3 pigeons, p=0.31; nRt: n=5 MIRS times in 3 pigeons, p=0.63; two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The MD simulation showed two remarkable absorption fingerprint peaks of K+ channels located between 33–37 THz, and 50–55 THz.
source: The MD simulation showed two remarkable absorption fingerprint peaks of K+ channels located between 33–37 THz, and 50–55 THz (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both fingerprint peaks are just out of the strong absorption spectral ranges of both water molecules and Na+ channels.
source: Both fingerprint peaks are just out of the strong absorption spectral ranges of both water molecules (Heyden et al., 2010) and Na+ channels.
evidence: The claim is based on simulation data and a citation to Heyden et al., 2010.

claim: The second absorption frequency of ~53 THz is consistent with prior research and well-studied.
source: The second absorption frequency of ~53 THz is consistent with prior research and well-studied (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: MIRS was mainly absorbed by −C=O groups at the inner wall of the filter region of K+ channels.
source: We note that the absorption fingerprint peak of −OH− groups at the filter region of Na+ channels are distant from ~34.88 THz (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that MIRS was mainly absorbed by −C=O groups at the inner wall of the filter region of K+ channels.
evidence: The claim is based on quantum chemistry calculations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: MIRS increased the PMF ratio of potassium ions by 1.15–1.4 folds at the exit site of K+ channels around ξ=1.1 nm when the field strength increased from 1.0 to 2.5 V/nm.
source: In the simulation, MIRS increased the PMF ratio of potassium ions by 1.15–1.4 folds at the exit site of K+ channels around ξ=1.1 nm when the field strength increased from 1.0 to 2.5 V/nm (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ratio of Na+ channels stayed near 1 at the exit site around ξ=0.5 nm under different field strengths.
source: At the same time, the ratio of Na+ channels stayed near 1 at the exit site around ξ=0.5 nm under different field strengths (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MIRS with 34.88 THz could be an useful approach to modulate the neural circuits and motor responses in a sensory input-dependent manner.
source: These findings suggest that MIRS with 34.88 THz could be an useful approach to modulate the neural circuits and motor responses in a sensory input-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental and simulation results presented in the study.

claim: MIRS could cause local thermal heat by water absorption, which changes capacitance of the transmembrane to excite cells.
source: A traditional explanation of these findings is that the MIRS could cause local thermal heat by water absorption, which changes capacitance of the transmembrane to excite cells (Shapiro et al., 2012), or activate thermosensitive TRPV channels to depolarize cells (Albert et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is presented as a traditional explanation with citations to prior research.

claim: MIRS does not have a thermally mediated effect on ion channels and neuronal functions when the distance was greater than 300 μm.
source: By contrast, experimental evidence in vitro demonstrates that MIRS does not have a thermally mediated effect on ion channels and neuronal functions, especially when the distance was greater than 300 μm (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: The distance between the MIRS fiber tip and recording sites was 848±351 µm (mean ± SD), limiting thermal changes within a range of 2 °C.
source: First, in our experiments, the distance between the MIRS fiber tip and recording sites was 848±351 µm (mean ± SD, Figure 1E), limiting thermal changes within a range of 2 °C (Tan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements and a citation to Tan et al., 2022.

claim: MIRS's multiplicative modulations of the action potential generation depended on the strength of current pulses in vitro, and an increase in K+ currents (not Na+ currents) could lead to gain modulation.
source: Recent research in brain slice found that MIRS's multiplicative modulations of the action potential generation depended on the strength of current pules in vitro, and an increase in K+currents (not Na+currents) could lead to gain modulation (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: MIRS could cause a shortened action potential duration (p<0.05).
source: The increased potassium ion flow by MIRS could cause a faster and/or earlier repolarization and lead to a shortened action potential duration (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, p<0.05, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Liu et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: MIRS could accelerate associative learning by stimulating the auditory cortex through opened or thinned intact skulls.
source: Recent research showed that MIRS could accelerate associative learning (Zhang et al., 2021) by stimulating the auditory cortex through opened or thinned intact skulls.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: The nLM relays visual information from the retina directly or indirectly to the vestibular cerebellum, the oculomotor cerebellum, the thalamus, the brainstem, and other brain areas.
source: Regarding connectivity, the nLM relays visual information from the retina directly or indirectly to the vestibular cerebellum, the oculomotor cerebellum, the thalamus, the brainstem, and other brain areas (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: These connections are integral to the nLM's role in eye and head movements, and many other behaviors, including postural and steering control.
source: These connections are integral to the nLM's role in eye and head movements, and many other behaviors, including postural and steering control (Cao et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2008b; Wylie, 2013; Ibbotson, 2017; Wylie et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The pretectal nLM is a crucial optokinetic nucleus responsible for encoding the horizontal optic flow and generating the OKN.
source: In birds, the pretectal nucleus lentiformis mesencephali (nLM) is a crucial optokinetic nucleus responsible for encoding the horizontal optic flow and generating the OKN.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the nLM's function.

claim: Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) occurs in two phases producing a characteristic irregular sawtooth waveform.
source: OKN occurs in two phases producing a characteristic irregular sawtooth waveform.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about OKN.

claim: A slow phase of pursuit eye movement closely tracks the moving field followed by a quick phase of ballistic saccadic eye movement that resets eyes to their primary position when they reach a maximal eccentricity.
source: A slow phase of pursuit eye movement closely tracks the moving field followed by a quick phase of ballistic saccadic eye movement that resets eyes to their primary position when they reach a maximal eccentricity (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about OKN and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The TeO is a principal destination of retinal ganglion axons and projects to the telencephalic entopallium via the nRt.
source: The TeO is a principal destination of retinal ganglion axons and projects to the telencephalic entopallium via the nRt.
evidence: The claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The ascending tectofugal pathway is considered homologous to the colliculo-pulvinar-cortical pathway in mammals.
source: The ascending tectofugal pathway is considered homologous to the colliculo-pulvinar-cortical pathway in mammals (Benowitz and Karten, 1976; Wang and Frost, 1992; Hellmann and Güntürkün, 2001; Reiner et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Both TeO and nRt nuclei are involved in visual information processing in birds, but not crucial for OKN generation.
source: Both nuclei are involved in visual information processing in birds, but not crucial for OKN generation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about these brain regions.

claim: The light spot diameter at a working distance of 850 μm can be about 1000 μm.
source: The light spot diameter at a working distance of 850 μm (mean distance between fiber tip and recorded neurons, Figure 1E) can be about 1000 μm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The laser could have a good chance to irradiate the pretectal nLM with a width of ~1000 μm.
source: Thus the laser could have a good chance to irradiate the pretectal nLM with a width of ~1000 μm (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the light spot diameter and the size of the nLM.

claim: MIRS can implement multiplication-like modulations on individual neurons in a sensory input-dependent manner.
source: Therefore, MIRS can implement multiplication-like modulations on individual neurons in a sensory input-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results showing bidirectional modulation depending on sensory input.

claim: MIRS could be a promising approach toward modulating neuronal functions for brain research and treating neurological diseases.
source: Our findings suggest that MIRS could be a promising approach toward modulating neuronal functions for brain research and treating neurological diseases.
evidence: The claim is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: MIRS can selectively activate or inhibit neuronal responses by controlling the strength of sensory inputs in an individual or population cells, without genetic manipulation.
source: Unlike the optogenetic stimulation that would require the delivery of the transgenes encoding the light-responsive proteins, MIRS can selectively activate or inhibit neuronal responses by controlling the strength of sensory inputs in an individual or population cells, without genetic manipulation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results and comparison with optogenetics.

claim: The 34.88 THz simulation frequency used in the study is closed to the maximum of the first peak of the K+ channels absorption spectrum, at least within half-height width of the fingerprint peak of 33–37 THz.
source: Note that the 34.88 THz simulation frequency we used in the initial results is closed to the maximum of the first peak of the K+ channels absorption spectrum, at least within half-height width of the fingerprint peak of 33–37 THz.
evidence: The claim is based on the simulation results and analysis of the absorption spectrum.

claim: The low-frequency oscillation mode corresponding to MIRS with 34.88 THz could involve almost all the −C=O groups in the filter structure vibrating in an in-plane bending manner.
source: Therefore, the low-frequency oscillation mode corresponding to MIRS with 34.88 THz could involve almost all the −C=O groups (similar to −C=O N-H) in the filter structure vibrating in an in-plane bending manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on quantum chemistry calculations and analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of MIRS with 34.88 THz could enhance the resonance absorption of K+ channels.
source: These data demonstrated that the effect of MIRS with 34.88 THz could enhance the resonance absorption of K+ channels.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the simulation data showing selective absorption by K+ channels.

claim: −C=O groups at the inner wall of K+ channels are frequency sensitive due to their collective resonance.
source: While −C=O groups at the inner wall of K+ channels are frequency sensitive due to their collective resonance, these effects seldom occur in Na+ channels or water molecules.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the simulation results showing differential absorption.

claim: Action potentials are generated and released in milliseconds, with approximately ~10^7 ions permeating across the membrane.
source: Action potentials are generated and released in milliseconds, with approximately ~107 ions permeating across the membrane.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about action potential generation.

claim: The ion permeation can be studied on the level of single one.
source: Thus, the ion permeation can be studied on the level of single one (Kopec et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kopec et al., 2018.

claim: The average permeation time for a single ion is on the order of nanosecond.
source: Here we have simulated the permeability of a single ion, with an average permeation time on the order of nanosecond (Kopec et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kopec et al., 2018.

claim: Increasing MIRS output power proportionally improves the efficiency of K+ permeability, in a manner that only weakly modulates Na+ channels.
source: Together, our simulations demonstrate a mechanism by which the K+ permeability can be selectively enhanced during MIRS with 34.88 THz. Increasing MIRS output power proportionally improves the efficiency of K+ permeability, in a manner that only weakly modulates Na+ channels.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the simulation results showing differential effects on K+ and Na+ channels.

claim: The enhancement of potassium permeability through K+ channels will lead to the changes in neuronal responses documented in the study.
source: This enhancement of potassium permeability through K+ channels will then lead to the changes in neuronal responses we document extensively above.
evidence: The claim is an inference linking the simulation results to the experimental observations.

claim: The increased potassium ion flow by MIRS could cause a faster and/or earlier repolarization.
source: The increased potassium ion flow by MIRS could cause a faster and/or earlier repolarization
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the known role of K+ channels in repolarization.

claim: Stimuli that more strongly drive a neuron might cause faster recovery from the inactivation of sodium channels and the prior action potential's refractory period.
source: As a result, stimuli that more strongly drive a neuron (i.e. motion in the preferred direction in our case) might cause faster recovery from the inactivation of sodium channels (Bean, 2007) and the prior action potential's refractory period.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mechanism of action potential generation and a citation to Bean, 2007.

claim: With stimuli that weakly drive or inhibit the neuron, the raising K+ permeability might hinder the depolarization and retard the threshold potential of a subsequent action potential, resulting in lower firing rates.
source: With stimuli that weakly drive or inhibit the neuron (i.e. motion in the null direction), the raising K+permeability might hinder the depolarization and retard the threshold potential of a subsequent action potential, resulting in lower firing rates.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mechanism of action potential generation.

claim: MIRS could preferentially modify permeation of K+ channels, leading to alternations of action potential generation in a manner of ongoing firing levels depended on sensory inputs.
source: Although our computational simulations do not simulate every stage, from ion channel dynamics to the generation of action potentials, our data are consistent with an ionic mechanism underlying MIRS: MIRS could preferentially modify permeation of K+channels, leading to alternations of action potential generation in a manner of ongoing firing levels depended on sensory inputs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined experimental and simulation results.

claim: MIRS causes a sensory-specific gain modulation in visual responses of the same neuron and behavioral performance.
source: Contrary to the unidirectional behavioural and neuronal effects of electrical stimulation (Figure 6D), MIRS causes a sensory-specific gain modulation in visual responses of the same neuron and behavioral performance (Figure 6C and E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6E.

claim: The MIRS effects on behavioral and neuronal responses were reversible after MIRS.
source: The MIRS effects on behavioral and neuronal responses were revisable after MIRS in our observations.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Pigeons highly depend on vision as creatures of flight.
source: Pigeons, as creatures of flight, highly depends on vision.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about pigeons.

claim: While pigeons fly or walk, the surrounding environment generates a large field of visual motion over the entire retina, known as optic flow.
source: While they fly or walk, the surrounding environment generates a large field of visual motion over the entire retina, known as optic flow (Gibson, 1951).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and a citation to Gibson, 1951.

claim: In the presence of visual motion, pigeons' eyes reflexively move to maintain stabilization of image on the retina, by ocular movements known as the optokinetic nystagmus (OKN).
source: In the presence of this visual motion, pigeons' eyes reflexively move to maintain stabilization of image on the retina, by ocular movements known as the optokinetic nystagmus (OKN).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about OKN.

claim: The quantum cascade mid-infrared laser (QCL) used had a constant radiation wavelength of 8.6 μm, and frequency of 34.88 THz.
source: We applied MIRS using a quantum cascade mid-infrared laser (QCL, Institute of Semiconductors, Chinese Academy of Sciences) with a constant radiation wavelength of 8.6 μm, and frequency of 34.88 THz.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup.

claim: The pulse train of MIRS lasted 30 or 120 seconds with a pulse width of 2 μs, a repetition frequency of 200 kHz, and a duty cycle of 40%.
source: The pulse train of MIRS lasted 30 or 120 seconds with a pulse width of 2 μs, a repetition frequency of 200 kHz, and a duty cycle of 40% (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental parameters shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Electrical stimulation was generated using an isolated pulse stimulator and applied for 120 s in the pretectal nLM, with parameters of 0.2 mA, 100 μs pulse width, 133 Hz.
source: Electrical stimulation was generated using an isolated pulse stimulator (A-M Systems, model 2100) and applied for 120 s in the pretectal nLM, with parameters of 0.2 mA, 100 μs pulse width, 133 Hz (Hao et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2018; Elias et al., 2021; Valverde et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup with citations to prior research using similar parameters.

claim: As the grating motion increased from 2 to 8 deg/s in preferred or null direction, average neuronal responses increased from ~45 to ~52 spikes/s or decreased from ~40 to ~33 spikes/s.
source: We found a gradation firing rate in recorded nLM neurons by grating speed: as the grating motion increased from 2 to 8 deg/s in preferred or null (negative velocity) direction, average neuronal responses increased from ~45 to~52 spikes/s or decreased from ~40 to~33 spikes/s, consistent with the results of prior research (Cao et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and consistent with a citation to Cao et al., 2004.
